\section{Probabilistic modal structures}\label{sec:setup}

Throughout, $S$ is a finite nonempty set of \emph{worlds} and $\iota$ an index set of
atomic propositions.

\begin{definition}[Probabilistic modal structure]
A \emph{probabilistic modal structure} $M$ on $S$ consists of a \emph{transition kernel}
$M(\cdot,\cdot):S\times S\to\mathbb{R}$ with $M(s,t)\ge 0$ and $\sum_{t\in S}M(s,t)=1$
for every $s$, together with a \emph{valuation} $V_M:\iota\times S\to[0,1]$.
\end{definition}

Allowing $V_M$ to take intermediate values costs nothing and includes the classical
two-valued case.

\begin{definition}[Formulas and depth]
The \emph{probabilistic modal formulas} over $\iota$ are generated by
\[
\varphi \;::=\; p \;\mid\; \neg\varphi \;\mid\; \varphi\wedge\psi \;\mid\; \Next\varphi
\qquad (p\in\iota),
\]
with \emph{modal depth} $\dpt(p)=0$, $\dpt(\neg\varphi)=\dpt(\varphi)$,
$\dpt(\varphi\wedge\psi)=\max(\dpt\varphi,\dpt\psi)$ and
$\dpt(\Next\varphi)=\dpt(\varphi)+1$. We write $\Next^{d}\varphi$ for the $d$-fold
application, so $\dpt(\Next^{d}\varphi)=d+\dpt(\varphi)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Truth-probability semantics]
For a structure $M$ set
\[
\sem{p}_M(s)=V_M(p,s),\qquad
\sem{\neg\varphi}_M(s)=1-\sem{\varphi}_M(s),
\]
\[
\sem{\varphi\wedge\psi}_M(s)=\min\bigl(\sem{\varphi}_M(s),\sem{\psi}_M(s)\bigr),
\qquad
\sem{\Next\varphi}_M(s)=\sum_{t\in S}M(s,t)\,\sem{\varphi}_M(t).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:range}
For every $\varphi$ and $s$ we have $0\le\sem{\varphi}_M(s)\le 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $\varphi$. Atoms lie in $[0,1]$ by hypothesis; negation and $\min$ preserve
$[0,1]$; for $\Next\varphi$, nonnegativity follows from nonnegativity of the kernel and
$\sum_t M(s,t)\sem{\varphi}_M(t)\le\sum_t M(s,t)=1$ from stochasticity.
\end{proof}

\section{Approximate analogies and transport}\label{sec:transport}

\subsection{The overlap defect}

\begin{definition}
For $P,Q:S\to\mathbb{R}$ the \emph{overlap defect} is
$\od(P,Q)=1-\sum_{t\in S}\min(P_t,Q_t)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Overlap defect is total variation]\label{lem:tv}
If $\sum_t P_t=\sum_t Q_t=1$ then $\od(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_{t}|P_t-Q_t|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Pointwise $|a-b|=a+b-2\min(a,b)$, by cases on $a\le b$ and $b\le a$; sum and use
$\sum P=\sum Q=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:odprops}
For probability vectors $P,Q,R$: \textup{(i)} $0\le\od(P,Q)\le 1$; \textup{(ii)}
$\od(P,R)\le\od(P,Q)+\od(Q,R)$; \textup{(iii)} $\od(P,Q)=0$ iff $P=Q$; \textup{(iv)}
$\od(P,Q)=\od(Q,P)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(i) $\sum_t\min(P_t,Q_t)\le\sum_t P_t=1$, and the minima are nonnegative. (ii) By
Lemma~\ref{lem:tv} it is the triangle inequality for $\ell^1$ applied termwise. (iii)
Vanishing forces $\sum_t|P_t-Q_t|=0$ and a sum of nonnegative terms vanishes only if
each does. (iv) $\min$ is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Approximate analogies}

\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$-approximate structural analogy]\label{def:analogy}
Let $M$ be a structure on $S$ and $N$ one on $S'$. An \emph{$\varepsilon$-approximate
structural analogy} $A:M\to N$ is a bijection $f:S\to S'$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(A)] $V_N(p,f(s))=V_M(p,s)$ for all $p\in\iota$, $s\in S$; and
\item[(D)] $\od\bigl(M(s,\cdot),\,N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr)\le\varepsilon$ for all $s\in S$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

Since $f$ is a bijection, $t\mapsto N(f(s),f(t))$ is again a probability vector, so (D)
says that after renaming every row of $M$'s kernel lies within total variation
$\varepsilon$ of the corresponding row of $N$'s. A $0$-approximate analogy is an
\emph{isomorphism}, by Lemma~\ref{lem:odprops}(iii).

\subsection{The one-step estimate}

\begin{lemma}[One-step estimate]\label{lem:onestep}
Let $P$ be a probability vector on $S$, $Q$ a nonnegative vector, and
$g,g':S\to\mathbb{R}$ with $g\le 1$ and $g'\ge 0$ pointwise. If $g(t)-g'(t)\le\delta$ for
all $t$, with $\delta\le 1$, and $\od(P,Q)\le\varepsilon$, then
\[
\sum_t P_t g(t)-\sum_t Q_t g'(t)\;\le\;\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $m_t=\min(P_t,Q_t)$ and $M_0=\sum_t m_t\ge 1-\varepsilon$, and split
\[
\sum_t P_tg(t)-\sum_t Q_tg'(t)
=\sum_t m_t\bigl(g(t)-g'(t)\bigr)+\sum_t (P_t-m_t)g(t)-\sum_t (Q_t-m_t)g'(t).
\]
The three terms are bounded by $M_0\delta$ (using $m_t\ge0$), by $1-M_0$ (using $g\le1$
and $\sum_t(P_t-m_t)=1-M_0$), and below by $0$ (using $Q_t\ge m_t$, $g'\ge0$). Their sum
is at most $M_0\delta+(1-M_0)\le\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta)$ since $1-M_0\le\varepsilon$
and $\delta\le1$.
\end{proof}

Interpretation: on the shared mass $M_0$ the expectations differ by at most $\delta$; on
the disagreeing mass $1-M_0\le\varepsilon$ only the trivial bound $1$ is available. Hence
the error recursion
\[
\delta\;\longmapsto\;\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta)\;=\;1-(1-\varepsilon)(1-\delta).
\]

\subsection{The transport theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative transport]\label{thm:transport}
Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ and let $f$ underlie an $\varepsilon$-approximate structural
analogy $M\to N$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ and every $s\in S$,
\[
\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_N(f(s))\bigr|
\;\le\; 1-(1-\varepsilon)^{\dpt\varphi}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $\varphi$. \emph{Atoms}: both sides agree by (A) and the bound is
$1-(1-\varepsilon)^0=0$. \emph{Negation}: the difference only changes sign, depth is
unchanged. \emph{Conjunction}: use
$|\min(a,b)-\min(a',b')|\le\max(|a-a'|,|b-b'|)$ together with monotonicity of
$d\mapsto 1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$ to lift both inductive bounds to the maximum of the
depths. \emph{Modality}: with
$\delta=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{\dpt\varphi}\in[0,1]$, put $P_t=M(s,t)$,
$Q_t=N(f(s),f(t))$, $g(t)=\sem{\varphi}_M(t)$, $g'(t)=\sem{\varphi}_N(f(t))$, reindex the
sum defining $\sem{\Next\varphi}_N(f(s))$ along $f$, and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:onestep} in
both directions (legitimate since $\od$ is symmetric). This yields the bound
$\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta)=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{\dpt\varphi+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Linear form]\label{cor:linear}
Under the same hypotheses,
$\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_N(f(s))\bigr|\le \dpt(\varphi)\cdot\varepsilon$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Bernoulli's inequality $(1+x)^d\ge1+dx$ with $x=-\varepsilon\ge-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact transport]
A $0$-approximate analogy preserves all truth probabilities.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Sharpness}

\begin{definition}[The extremal family]\label{def:extremal}
On $S=\{\F,\T\}$ with a single atom $a$ satisfying $V(a,\T)=1$, $V(a,\F)=0$: the
\emph{exact system} $E$ has both worlds absorbing; the \emph{leaky system}
$L_\varepsilon$ ($0\le\varepsilon\le1$) has $L_\varepsilon(\T,\T)=1-\varepsilon$,
$L_\varepsilon(\T,\F)=\varepsilon$ and $L_\varepsilon(\F,\F)=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:extremal}
The identity is an $\varepsilon$-approximate analogy $E\to L_\varepsilon$, with one-step
overlap defect exactly $\varepsilon$ at $\T$ and $0$ at $\F$. Moreover
$\sem{\Next^{d}a}_E(\T)=1$, $\sem{\Next^{d}a}_{L_\varepsilon}(\T)=(1-\varepsilon)^d$ and
$\sem{\Next^{d}a}_{L_\varepsilon}(\F)=0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Direct computation for the defect. For the values, induct on $d$: the world $\F$ is
absorbing with $a$ false, so its value is $0$ at every depth, whence the recursion at
$\T$ reads $x_{d+1}=(1-\varepsilon)x_d$ with $x_0=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment of the geometric modulus]\label{thm:sharp}
For every $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$ and every $d\ge0$,
\[
\bigl|\sem{\Next^{d}a}_E(\T)-\sem{\Next^{d}a}_{L_\varepsilon}(\T)\bigr|
=1-(1-\varepsilon)^d,
\]
so the bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:transport} is attained at every depth.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The linear bound is never attained beyond depth one]\label{thm:notattained}
For $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $d\ge2$ one has $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d<d\varepsilon$ strictly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $d$. For $d=2$ the gap is $\varepsilon^2>0$. For the step write
$1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d+1}=\bigl(1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d}\bigr)+\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)^{d}$
and use the inductive strict inequality with $(1-\varepsilon)^d<1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[First-order sharpness]\label{thm:firstorder}
For $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ and $d\ge0$,
\[
d\varepsilon-\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\varepsilon^{2}\;\le\;1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d},
\]
i.e.\ $d\varepsilon-\bigl(1-(1-\varepsilon)^d\bigr)\le\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\varepsilon^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $d$ using $a_{d+1}=a_d+\varepsilon(1-a_d)$ for
$a_d=1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, combined with the crude bound $a_d\le d\varepsilon$ of
Corollary~\ref{cor:linear}.
\end{proof}

Thus the linear modulus is confirmed as a bound, refuted as an equality, and vindicated
to first order, the discrepancy being $O(d^2\varepsilon^2)$.

\section{The metric groupoid of approximate analogies}\label{sec:groupoid}

\begin{proposition}[Groupoid structure]\label{prop:groupoid}
Let $M,N,K$ be probabilistic modal structures.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The identity is a $0$-approximate analogy $M\to M$.
\item An $\varepsilon$-analogy is an $\varepsilon'$-analogy whenever
$\varepsilon\le\varepsilon'$.
\item If $f$ underlies an $\varepsilon$-analogy $M\to N$, then $f^{-1}$ underlies an
$\varepsilon$-analogy $N\to M$.
\item If $f$ underlies an $\varepsilon_1$-analogy $M\to N$ and $g$ an
$\varepsilon_2$-analogy $N\to K$, then $g\circ f$ underlies an
$(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)$-analogy $M\to K$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) $\od(P,P)=0$. (2) Immediate. (3) Reindex the defect sum along $f$ and use symmetry
of $\min$. (4) The atomic condition composes; for the defect fix $s$ and set
$P_t=M(s,t)$, $Q_t=N(f(s),f(t))$, $R_t=K(gf(s),gf(t))$, so that
$\od(P,Q)\le\varepsilon_1$ directly and $\od(Q,R)\le\varepsilon_2$ after reindexing the
defect of $g$ at $f(s)$ along $f$; conclude with Lemma~\ref{lem:odprops}(ii).
\end{proof}

Thus approximate analogies form a groupoid whose arrows carry an additive $[0,1]$-valued
grading given by total variation, with identities of grade $0$ and grade-preserving
inversion.

\begin{corollary}[Composite transport]\label{cor:comptransport}
If $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\ge0$ with $\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\le1$ then along
the composite,
$\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_K(g(f(s)))\bigr|
\le 1-\bigl(1-(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)\bigr)^{\dpt\varphi}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Two-step holonomy]\label{cor:holonomy2}
If $f:M\to N$ and $g:N\to M$ are $\varepsilon$-analogies with $2\varepsilon\le1$ then
$\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_M(g(f(s)))\bigr|\le1-(1-2\varepsilon)^{\dpt\varphi}$.
If both are exact, the two sides of the difference coincide: exact loops have trivial
semantic holonomy.
\end{corollary}

\section{The analogy distance}\label{sec:metric}

Fix a finite nonempty world set $S$ and consider structures on $S$, so that renamings are
permutations of $S$.

\begin{definition}[Atom-preserving renamings]
$\AtomPerm(M,N)=\{f\in\Sym(S): V_N(p,f(s))=V_M(p,s)\ \text{for all }p,s\}$.
\end{definition}

This is a finite set containing the bijection of every approximate analogy $M\to N$.

\begin{definition}[Cost of a renaming]
$\cost_{M,N}(f)=\max_{s\in S}\od\bigl(M(s,\cdot),N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:cost}
$0\le\cost_{M,N}(f)\le1$, and $f$ underlies an $\varepsilon$-approximate analogy $M\to N$
if and only if $f\in\AtomPerm(M,N)$ and $\cost_{M,N}(f)\le\varepsilon$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The bounds are Lemma~\ref{lem:odprops}(i) at the maximising world (the maximum over a
finite nonempty set is attained); the characterisation is
Definition~\ref{def:analogy} read componentwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Analogy distance]\label{def:dist}
\[
d(M,N)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\min_{f\in\AtomPerm(M,N)}\cost_{M,N}(f), & \AtomPerm(M,N)\neq\emptyset,\\[2mm]
1, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

The convention in the degenerate case is harmless: with no atom-preserving renaming there
is no analogy of any defect, and $1$ is the maximum possible defect.

\begin{theorem}[Range]
$d(M,N)\in[0,1]$ for all $M,N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment]\label{thm:attained}
If $\AtomPerm(M,N)\neq\emptyset$ then there is $f^\star\in\AtomPerm(M,N)$ with
$\cost_{M,N}(f^\star)=d(M,N)$, and $f^\star$ underlies an honest $d(M,N)$-approximate
structural analogy $M\to N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The minimum in Definition~\ref{def:dist} ranges over a nonempty finite set, hence is
attained at some $f^\star$; the defect condition at each world then holds with bound
$\cost_{M,N}(f^\star)=d(M,N)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cost}.
\end{proof}

This is the crux: because the atomic condition rigidifies the search space to a finite
set, the infimum defining $d$ is a \emph{minimum}.

\begin{theorem}[Least admissible defect]\label{thm:leastdefect}
If $\AtomPerm(M,N)\neq\emptyset$ then for every $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\exists\;\varepsilon\text{-approximate analogy } M\to N
\iff d(M,N)\le\varepsilon .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) Its bijection lies in $\AtomPerm(M,N)$ with cost $\le\varepsilon$.
($\Leftarrow$) Take the optimal analogy of Theorem~\ref{thm:attained} and weaken.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The metric axioms}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:metricaxioms}
For all structures $M,N,K$ on $S$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $d(M,M)=0$;
\item $d(M,N)=d(N,M)$;
\item if $\AtomPerm(M,N)$ and $\AtomPerm(N,K)$ are nonempty then
$d(M,K)\le d(M,N)+d(N,K)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each axiom is a groupoid operation applied to optimal analogies. (1) The identity is a
$0$-analogy. (2) $f\mapsto f^{-1}$ is a bijection $\AtomPerm(M,N)\to\AtomPerm(N,M)$;
inverting the optimal analogy gives an analogy of the same defect in the other direction,
and symmetrically; in the degenerate case both sides equal $1$. (3) Compose the two
optimal analogies (Proposition~\ref{prop:groupoid}(4)) and apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:leastdefect}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The zero set is isomorphism}

\begin{definition}[Isomorphism]
An \emph{isomorphism} $M\to N$ is a permutation $f$ of $S$ with $V_N(p,f(s))=V_M(p,s)$
for all $p,s$ and $N(f(s),f(t))=M(s,t)$ for all $s,t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:zeroset}
If $\AtomPerm(M,N)\neq\emptyset$ then $d(M,N)=0$ if and only if $M$ and $N$ are
isomorphic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) An isomorphism has all overlap defects $\od(P,P)=0$, hence is a
$0$-analogy. ($\Rightarrow$) The optimal renaming $f^\star$ has defect at most
$d(M,N)=0$ and at least $0$ at every $s$, so
$\od\bigl(M(s,\cdot),N(f^\star(s),f^\star(\cdot))\bigr)=0$; both arguments are
probability vectors, so Lemma~\ref{lem:odprops}(iii) gives
$N(f^\star(s),f^\star(t))=M(s,t)$ for all $t$. As $f^\star$ preserves atoms, it is an
isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$d$ descends to a genuine $[0,1]$-valued metric on isomorphism classes of probabilistic
modal structures on a fixed finite world set.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The optimal modulus of continuity}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal transport bound]\label{thm:opttransport}
If $\AtomPerm(M,N)\neq\emptyset$ and $f^\star$ is the optimal renaming, then for every
$\varphi$ and $s$,
\[
\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_N(f^\star(s))\bigr|
\;\le\;1-\bigl(1-d(M,N)\bigr)^{\dpt\varphi}
\;\le\;\dpt(\varphi)\cdot d(M,N).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:transport} to the optimal analogy, whose defect lies in $[0,1]$,
and Corollary~\ref{cor:linear} for the linear form.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $d(M,N)=0$ then $\sem{\varphi}_M(s)=\sem{\varphi}_N(f^\star(s))$ for all $\varphi,s$.
\end{corollary}

Theorem~\ref{thm:opttransport} states that the map
$\Phi_d:M\mapsto\bigl(\sem{\varphi}_M\bigr)_{\dpt\varphi\le d}$ is uniformly continuous
for $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ with modulus $\omega_d(x)=1-(1-x)^d$ in the supremum norm. The next
result shows this cannot be improved.

\begin{theorem}[Exact distance on the extremal family]\label{thm:distextremal}
For the family of Definition~\ref{def:extremal} and any $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$,
\[
d\bigl(E,L_\varepsilon\bigr)=\varepsilon .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\le$) The identity is an $\varepsilon$-analogy (Lemma~\ref{lem:extremal}).
($\ge$) The atom $a$ has value $1$ at $\T$ and $0$ at $\F$, so the only atom-preserving
permutation of $\{\F,\T\}$ is the identity; hence
$d(E,L_\varepsilon)=\cost(\mathrm{id})\ge\od\bigl(E(\T,\cdot),L_\varepsilon(\T,\cdot)\bigr)
=\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The modulus is exact]
For every $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$ and $d\ge0$ there are structures at analogy distance
$\varepsilon$ and a formula of depth $d$ whose truth probabilities differ by exactly
$1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$. Hence $\omega_d$ is the modulus of continuity of $\Phi_d$, not
merely an upper envelope.
\end{corollary}

\section{Networks of analogies and semantic holonomy}\label{sec:networks}

Let $M_0,M_1,\dots$ be structures on a common world set and let $A_i$ be an
$\varepsilon_i$-approximate analogy $M_i\to M_{i+1}$, with composite bijection $F_k$
after $k$ steps.

\begin{proposition}[Defects add along a path]
For each $k$, $F_k$ underlies an approximate analogy $M_0\to M_k$ of defect
$\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $k$, with Proposition~\ref{prop:groupoid}(1) for $k=0$ and
Proposition~\ref{prop:groupoid}(4) together with weakening for the step.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Network transport]
If $\varepsilon_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i\le1$ then
\[
\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(s)-\sem{\varphi}_{M_k}(F_k(s))\bigr|
\le 1-\Bigl(1-\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i\Bigr)^{\dpt\varphi}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Semantic holonomy]
A \emph{cycle} is a chain with $M_k=M_0$; then $F_k$ is a permutation of the worlds of
$M_0$, and the \emph{semantic holonomy} at $\varphi,s$ is
$\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(s)-\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(F_k(s))\bigr|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Holonomy bound]
The semantic holonomy of a cycle is at most
$1-\bigl(1-\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i\bigr)^{\dpt\varphi}$, hence at most
$\dpt(\varphi)\cdot\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cycles are coherent]\label{thm:coherent}
If every $\varepsilon_i=0$ then $\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(s)=\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(F_k(s))$ for
all $\varphi,s$. Consequently, if $I:S\to\mathbb{R}$ is an interpretation that factors
through modal theories --- that is, $\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(s)=\sem{\varphi}_{M_0}(t)$ for
all $\varphi$ implies $I(s)=I(t)$ --- then $I(s)=I(F_k(s))$ for every $s$: meanings are
globally coherent around the loop.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Non-vacuity]
The bound is not empty. On $\{\F,\T\}$ with a single atom true only at $\T$, let the first
system send every world to $\T$ and the second send every world to $\F$. The identity is a
$1$-approximate analogy in both directions, and $\sem{\Next a}$ equals $1$ in the first
system and $0$ in the second: a two-arrow loop of total defect $1$ destroys all depth-one
information, so the holonomy bound is attained at total defect $1$.
\end{remark}

\section{Observational resolution}\label{sec:resolution}

\subsection{The resolution gap}

\begin{definition}
On $\{\F,\T\}$ with all atoms identically $1$, let $\mathrm{Id}$ be the system in which
each world has a self-loop and $\mathrm{Sw}$ the system in which the two worlds swap.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Resolution gap]\label{thm:gap}
Every modal formula has the same truth probability at every world of $\mathrm{Id}$ and of
$\mathrm{Sw}$; yet $d(\mathrm{Id},\mathrm{Sw})=1$, so there is no
$\varepsilon$-approximate analogy between them with $\varepsilon<1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Since every atom is identically $1$, an induction shows that each
$\sem{\varphi}$ is a constant function of the world, with the same constant in both
systems, because $\Next$ averages a constant against a stochastic row. For the second
half, both permutations of a two-element set preserve the constant valuation, and for
either the transported kernel of $\mathrm{Sw}$ is again the swap kernel, whose rows are
mutually singular with those of $\mathrm{Id}$: overlap defect $1$ at every world.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Counting does not help}

Consider \emph{graded modalities} $\nabla_k\varphi$, read ``at least $k$ successors of
positive probability satisfy $\varphi$'', interpreted two-valued (an atom holds where its
truth probability is positive). Graded truth is invariant under exact structural
analogies, so the language is sound for classification; but it is too weak.

\begin{theorem}[Counting is blind on deterministic systems]\label{thm:graded}
Let $M,N$ have deterministic kernels (each world with exactly one successor of positive
probability) and constant atomic valuations, on arbitrary finite nonempty world sets with
arbitrary successor functions. Then every graded formula has the same truth value at
every world of $M$ and of $N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on the graded formula. Atoms and Booleans are immediate from constancy. For
$\nabla_k\varphi$, each world has exactly one positive-probability successor, so the
relevant count is $1$ if $\varphi$ holds there and $0$ otherwise; by induction $\varphi$
has a constant truth value across both systems, so the count is uniform and
$\nabla_k\varphi$ holds everywhere or nowhere, identically in both systems.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The pair $(\mathrm{Id},\mathrm{Sw})$ is graded-equivalent yet at analogy distance $1$: no
graded language classifies pointed structures up to isomorphism.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
What separates $\mathrm{Id}$ from $\mathrm{Sw}$ is not a counting observation but the
self-reference predicate $M(s,s)>0$ --- a fixed-point property, invariant under exact
analogies but inexpressible by counting. The missing resolution is a fixed-point
phenomenon, not a multiplicity phenomenon.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The nominal case: sharp approximate Hennessy--Milner}

\begin{definition}[Nominal structure]
A structure $M$ on $S$ with atom set $\iota=S$ is \emph{nominal} for a bijection $\kappa$
if $V_M(u,v)=1$ when $v=\kappa(u)$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[The naming bijection is forced]\label{prop:forced}
If $M$ is nominal for the identity and $N$ for $\kappa$, then every approximate analogy
$M\to N$, of any defect, has underlying bijection exactly $\kappa$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply the atomic condition to the atom $s$ at the world $s$: it reads $V_N(s,f(s))=1$,
and $V_N(s,\cdot)$ equals $1$ only at $\kappa(s)$.
\end{proof}

In a nominal structure the depth-one observations are exactly the kernel entries:
$\sem{\Next u}_M(s)=M(s,u)$.

\begin{theorem}[Approximate Hennessy--Milner theorem, nominal case]\label{thm:hm}
Let $M,N$ be nominal structures on $n=|S|$ worlds, for the identity and for $\kappa$
respectively, and suppose
$\bigl|\sem{\Next u}_M(s)-\sem{\Next u}_N(\kappa(s))\bigr|\le\eta$ for all $u,s$. Then
$\kappa$ underlies an $(n\eta/2)$-approximate structural analogy $M\to N$; hence,
provided $n\eta/2\le1$,
\[
\bigl|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_N(\kappa(s))\bigr|
\le 1-\bigl(1-n\eta/2\bigr)^{\dpt\varphi}\le\dpt(\varphi)\cdot\frac{n\eta}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The hypothesis says every kernel entry moves by at most $\eta$, so a row moves by at most
$n\eta$ in $\ell^1$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:tv} the overlap defect is half of this. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:transport} and Corollary~\ref{cor:linear}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimality of the dimension factor]\label{thm:hmsharp}
For every $m\ge1$, writing $n=2m$, and every $\eta$ with $0\le\eta\le1/(2m)$, there are
nominal structures $U$ (uniform) and $T$ (tilted) on $n$ worlds such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\bigl|\sem{\Next u}_U(s)-\sem{\Next u}_T(s)\bigr|=\eta$ for \emph{every} pair
$(u,s)$; and
\item every $\varepsilon$-approximate analogy $U\to T$ satisfies $\varepsilon\ge n\eta/2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take worlds $\{+,-\}\times\{1,\dots,m\}$, let $U(s,t)=1/n$ and
$T(s,t)=1/n+\eta$ for $t$ in the positive half, $1/n-\eta$ otherwise; admissibility keeps
$T$ nonnegative and the halves have equal size so rows sum to $1$. Both are nominal for
the identity, so (1) is immediate. For (2), the naming bijection is forced
(Proposition~\ref{prop:forced}) and the overlap defect of a row is $m\eta=n\eta/2$, since
the pointwise minimum is the $T$-entry on the negative half and the common value $1/n$ on
the positive half.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Recovery of a finite nominal probabilistic structure from depth-one observations is
Lipschitz from the $\ell^\infty$ observation metric to the analogy metric, with Lipschitz
constant exactly $n/2$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms and complexity}\label{sec:algorithms}

Let $n=|S|$ and $a=|\iota|$.

\begin{algorithmbox}[Overlap defect]
Given rows $P,Q\in\mathbb{R}^n$, return $1-\sum_t\min(P_t,Q_t)$; cost $\Theta(n)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:tv} this equals $\tfrac12\lVert P-Q\rVert_1$; the $\min$ form is
numerically preferable, avoiding cancellation for nearly identical rows.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Cost of a renaming]
Given $M,N,f$, return $\max_s\od\bigl(M(s,\cdot),N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr)$; cost
$\Theta(n^2)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Analogy distance by exhaustive search]\label{alg:dist}
Enumerate $f\in\Sym(S)$; discard $f$ unless it preserves atoms (an $O(an)$ test);
evaluate the previous algorithm and keep the minimum and its argmin. Cost
$O(n!\,(an+n^2))$. Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:attained}: the minimum over this
finite set \emph{is} the distance and the argmin \emph{is} an optimal analogy; the output
is exact.
\end{algorithmbox}

The atomic filter is a strong pruning device: its effect is to restrict $f$ to
permutations respecting the partition of $S$ into \emph{atomic types} (worlds with equal
atomic valuation vectors). If the types have sizes $n_1,\dots,n_r$ then
$|\AtomPerm(M,N)|$ is $0$ or $\prod_i n_i!$; in the nominal case all types are
singletons, so the distance is computed in $\Theta(n^2)$.

\begin{algorithmbox}[Type-refined search]
Compute atomic types of $M$ and of $N$; if the multisets of type sizes differ, return $1$
(no analogy exists). Otherwise enumerate only type-respecting bijections; cost
$O\bigl(\prod_i n_i!\cdot n^2\bigr)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Certified transport bound]
Given $M,N,\varphi$: compute $d(M,N)$ and $f^\star$; evaluate $\sem{\varphi}$ in both
systems by dynamic programming over subformulas ($\Theta(|\varphi|n^2)$ for modal cases,
$\Theta(|\varphi|n)$ otherwise); report the observed discrepancy against the certified
bound $1-(1-d(M,N))^{\dpt\varphi}$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Network holonomy audit]
Given a finite graph of systems with an analogy on each edge, compute a spanning tree and
a cycle basis; for each basis cycle sum the local defects and report the holonomy bound
$1-(1-\sum\varepsilon_i)^{d}$. A cycle of total defect $0$ is certified coherent
(Theorem~\ref{thm:coherent}); a cycle whose bound exceeds tolerance is flagged. Cost is
dominated by $O(|E|)$ distance computations.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{remark}[Hardness caveat]
Exact minimisation over renamings contains graph isomorphism as the special case $d=0$
with $0/1$ kernels, so no polynomial algorithm should be expected in general. The
practical route is type refinement combined with isomorphism-style partition refinement
using row-distance invariants.
\end{remark}

\section{Applications}\label{sec:applications}

\textbf{Model reduction with certified error.} Replacing a system $M$ by a surrogate $N$
on the same world set, the analogy distance yields an \emph{a priori} guarantee: every
depth-$d$ property has its probability preserved to within $1-(1-d(M,N))^d$. Since the
modulus saturates rather than growing linearly, the guarantee is informative for far
larger $d$ than a linear budget suggests.

\textbf{Auditing analogical inference.} When an argument transfers reasoning across a
chain of models, network transport gives an error budget additive in the local defects
and geometric in the depth; the holonomy bound turns loops into an auditable diagnostic,
flagging exactly the places where ``the same'' object receives inconsistent meanings.

\textbf{Sensitivity of Markov-chain queries.} Depth-$d$ formulas encode finite-horizon
queries: $\Next^{d}p$ is a horizon-$d$ reachability probability, and Boolean combinations
build finite-horizon safety and until-like properties. The transport theorem is a
perturbation bound for such queries under row-wise total-variation perturbation, with a
sharp constant.

\textbf{System identification.} Theorem~\ref{thm:hm} bounds how well a kernel can be
reconstructed from finite-horizon observations, and Theorem~\ref{thm:hmsharp} shows the
constant $n/2$ is unavoidable: to estimate a kernel to total-variation accuracy
$\varepsilon$ one needs entrywise observational accuracy $2\varepsilon/n$.

\textbf{Limits of behavioural testing.} Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} cautions any pipeline that
infers structure from black-box behaviour: without world-identifying observations,
distinct structures can be behaviourally identical at every horizon, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:graded} shows that counting power does not help. The informative
enrichment is self-reference.

\section{Discussion and future work}\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{What the results say}
Three theses emerge. \emph{Compounding is geometric}: the correct modulus is
$1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, not $d\varepsilon$; the two agree to first order but the geometric
modulus respects the fact that truth probabilities live in $[0,1]$, so error saturates
rather than accumulating without bound. \emph{Approximate sameness is metric, and the
optimum is realised}: the atomic condition confines the optimisation to finitely many
candidates, so the infimum is a minimum witnessed by an explicit renaming, the metric
axioms follow formally from the groupoid structure, and the zero set is exactly
isomorphism. \emph{Sameness depends on the observational language}: structural analogy
and modal truth-probability equivalence differ already on two worlds, counting modalities
do not bridge the gap, and naming does, at depth one, with the sharp constant $n/2$.

\subsection{Limitations}
The distance compares structures on a \emph{common} world set via permutations; different
sizes require padding or a coupling-based generalisation. It is a worst-case-over-worlds
quantity, so an averaged or initial-distribution-weighted variant would be less brittle.
Being bounded by $1$, it cannot distinguish ``very different'' from ``maximally
different'': mutually singular kernels are all at distance $1$. Exact computation is
isomorphism-hard in general.

\subsection{Open problems}

\begin{problem}[Couplings rather than bijections]
Replace the renaming by a coupling of world sets, obtaining a Kantorovich-style analogy
distance between systems of different sizes. Is the infimum still attained, and is the
transport modulus still $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A behavioural metric]
Define $\rho(M,N)=\sup_\varphi\sup_s|\sem{\varphi}_M(s)-\sem{\varphi}_N(\sigma(s))|$ over
a canonical correspondence $\sigma$. Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} gives pairs with
$\rho=0<d=1$. Characterise the pairs where $\rho$ and $d$ agree and quantify the gap.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Fixed-point observations]
Enrich the language with self-reference. What is the exact expressive threshold at which
observational equivalence coincides with $d(M,N)=0$?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Discounted and averaged moduli]
Determine the exact modulus in a discounted setting, with the corresponding extremal
family.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Networks beyond cycle bases]
Formulate a groupoid-cohomological obstruction whose vanishing is equivalent to global
coherence of meanings across a network of approximate analogies, and relate its norm to
the maximum holonomy over a cycle basis.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Statistical estimation]
Given samples rather than exact kernels, estimate $d(M,N)$ with confidence intervals;
combine Theorem~\ref{thm:hmsharp} with concentration for total variation to obtain
sample-complexity bounds.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Summary of the main results}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.30\textwidth}p{0.62\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Statement} & \textbf{Content}\\
\midrule
Transport & depth-$d$ error $\le 1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$ along an $\varepsilon$-analogy\\
Sharpness & attained by the two-state leaking family at every depth\\
Linear bound & $\le d\varepsilon$ always; strict for $d\ge2$; sharp to first order\\
Groupoid & identities exact, inverses isometric, composition additive\\
Attainment & the infimum defining $d(M,N)$ is a minimum with explicit optimal renaming\\
Metric & $d\in[0,1]$, symmetric, triangle inequality, zero set $=$ isomorphism\\
Optimal continuity & modulus $1-(1-d(M,N))^{d}$, attained since
$d(E,L_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$\\

optimal\\

The Analogy Distance on Finite Probabilistic Transition Systems
================================================================

A self-contained numerical companion to the theory of epsilon-approximate
structural analogies between finite probabilistic transition systems.

Everything is implemented from scratch with the Python standard library only
(no numpy, no scipy), so the script runs anywhere.

What is demonstrated
--------------------
1.  The overlap defect  1 - sum_t min(P_t, Q_t)  equals the total variation
    distance  (1/2) * sum_t |P_t - Q_t|  of two probability vectors.
2.  The transport theorem: along an epsilon-approximate analogy the truth
    probability of a depth-d formula moves by at most  1 - (1 - eps)^d,
    and this geometric modulus is attained by an explicit two-state family.
3.  The conjectured linear modulus  d * eps  is a valid but strictly weaker
    bound for d >= 2, sharp only to first order in eps.
4.  The analogy distance  d(M, N) = min over atom-preserving renamings of the
    worst-case one-step overlap defect: an attained minimum, a metric, with
    zero set exactly isomorphism.
5.  The exact value  d(exact, leaky(eps)) = eps  on the extremal family.
6.  The approximate Hennessy-Milner constant  n * eta / 2  and its optimality.
7.  The resolution gap: two systems with identical modal truth probabilities
    at every depth but analogy distance 1.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]

TOL = 1e-9


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Probability vectors, overlap defect, total variation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The overlap defect  1 - sum_t min(p_t, q_t)  of two vectors."""
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def total_variation(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Total variation distance  (1/2) * sum_t |p_t - q_t|."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Probabilistic modal structures and their formulas
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class PSystem:
    """A finite probabilistic modal structure.

    `step[s][t]` is the probability of moving from world s to world t; every
    row is a probability vector.  `val[p][s]` in [0,1] is the truth
    probability of the atom p at the world s.
    """

    def __init__(self, step: Matrix, val: Dict[str, Vector], name: str = "M") -> None:
        self.n: int = len(step)
        self.step: Matrix = [list(row) for row in step]
        self.val: Dict[str, Vector] = {p: list(v) for p, v in val.items()}
        self.name: str = name
        for s, row in enumerate(self.step):
            assert len(row) == self.n, "kernel must be square"
            assert all(x >= -TOL for x in row), "kernel must be nonnegative"
            assert abs(sum(row) - 1.0) < 1e-8, f"row {s} of {name} is not stochastic"
        for p, v in self.val.items():
            assert all(-TOL <= x <= 1.0 + TOL for x in v), f"atom {p} out of [0,1]"


# Formulas are nested tuples:
#   ("atom", p) | ("neg", phi) | ("conj", phi, psi) | ("next", phi)
Formula = tuple


def atom(p: str) -> Formula:
    return ("atom", p)


def neg(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("neg", phi)


def conj(phi: Formula, psi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("conj", phi, psi)


def nxt(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("next", phi)


def next_iter(d: int, phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    """The modality `next` applied d times."""
    for _ in range(d):
        phi = nxt(phi)
    return phi


def depth(phi: Formula) -> int:
    """Modal depth: the number of nested one-step observations."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return 0
    if kind == "neg":
        return depth(phi[1])
    if kind == "conj":
        return max(depth(phi[1]), depth(phi[2]))
    if kind == "next":
        return depth(phi[1]) + 1
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


def evaluate(m: PSystem, phi: Formula, s: int) -> float:
    """Truth probability of phi at the world s of m."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return m.val[phi[1]][s]
    if kind == "neg":
        return 1.0 - evaluate(m, phi[1], s)
    if kind == "conj":
        return min(evaluate(m, phi[1], s), evaluate(m, phi[2], s))
    if kind == "next":
        return sum(m.step[s][t] * evaluate(m, phi[1], t) for t in range(m.n))
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Approximate analogies and the analogy distance
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def preserves_atoms(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does the renaming f of worlds preserve every atomic truth probability?"""
    if set(m.val) != set(n.val):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.val[p][f[s]] - m.val[p][s]) < 1e-9
        for p in m.val
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_cost(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Worst-case one-step overlap defect produced by the renaming f."""
    return max(
        overlap_defect(m.step[s], [n.step[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(m.n)])
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_distance(m: PSystem, n: PSystem) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[int, ...] | None]:
    """The analogy distance and an optimal renaming attaining it.

    d(M, N) = min { analogy_cost(M, N, f) : f an atom-preserving renaming },
    with the junk value 1 (and no witness) if no such renaming exists.
    Brute force over all n! renamings; feasible for n <= 8.
    """
    assert m.n == n.n, "systems must have the same number of worlds"
    best: float = 1.0
    witness: Tuple[int, ...] | None = None
    found = False
    for f in permutations(range(m.n)):
        if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
            continue
        c = analogy_cost(m, n, f)
        if not found or c < best:
            best, witness, found = c, f, True
    return (best, witness) if found else (1.0, None)


def is_isomorphism(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does f preserve atoms and carry the kernel of m onto that of n exactly?"""
    if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.step[f[s]][f[t]] - m.step[s][t]) < 1e-9
        for s in range(m.n)
        for t in range(m.n)
    )


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The extremal two-state family
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exact_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two absorbing worlds; the atom holds at world 1 and fails at world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name="exact")


def leaky_system(eps: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eps leaks out of world 1 into the absorbing world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [eps, 1.0 - eps]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name=f"leaky({eps})")


def geometric_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - eps) ** d


def linear_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return d * eps


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The Hennessy-Milner extremal family on n = 2m worlds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nominal_uniform(m: int) -> PSystem:
    """Uniform kernel on n = 2m worlds, with one nominal atom per world."""
    n = 2 * m
    step = [[1.0 / n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"uniform({n})")


def nominal_tilted(m: int, eta: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eta is moved from each 'negative' world to a
    'positive' one.  Worlds 0..m-1 are positive, worlds m..2m-1 negative."""
    n = 2 * m
    row = [1.0 / n + (eta if j < m else -eta) for j in range(n)]
    step = [list(row) for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"tilted({n},{eta})")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The resolution gap
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def identity_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds, each with a self-loop; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="two loops")


def swap_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds forming a 2-cycle; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="2-cycle")


def all_formulas(atoms: Sequence[str], max_depth: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """All formulas over the given atoms up to the given modal depth
    (a finite generating family: atoms, negations, conjunctions, nexts)."""
    level: List[Formula] = [atom(p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[Formula] = list(level)
    for _ in range(max_depth):
        new: List[Formula] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(nxt(phi))
            new.append(neg(phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(conj(phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]

TOL = 1e-9


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Probability vectors, overlap defect, total variation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The overlap defect  1 - sum_t min(p_t, q_t)  of two vectors."""
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def total_variation(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Total variation distance  (1/2) * sum_t |p_t - q_t|."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Probabilistic modal structures and their formulas
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class PSystem:
    """A finite probabilistic modal structure.

    `step[s][t]` is the probability of moving from world s to world t; every
    row is a probability vector.  `val[p][s]` in [0,1] is the truth
    probability of the atom p at the world s.
    """

    def __init__(self, step: Matrix, val: Dict[str, Vector], name: str = "M") -> None:
        self.n: int = len(step)
        self.step: Matrix = [list(row) for row in step]
        self.val: Dict[str, Vector] = {p: list(v) for p, v in val.items()}
        self.name: str = name
        for s, row in enumerate(self.step):
            assert len(row) == self.n, "kernel must be square"
            assert all(x >= -TOL for x in row), "kernel must be nonnegative"
            assert abs(sum(row) - 1.0) < 1e-8, f"row {s} of {name} is not stochastic"
        for p, v in self.val.items():
            assert all(-TOL <= x <= 1.0 + TOL for x in v), f"atom {p} out of [0,1]"


# Formulas are nested tuples:
#   ("atom", p) | ("neg", phi) | ("conj", phi, psi) | ("next", phi)
Formula = tuple


def atom(p: str) -> Formula:
    return ("atom", p)


def neg(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("neg", phi)


def conj(phi: Formula, psi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("conj", phi, psi)


def nxt(phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    return ("next", phi)


def next_iter(d: int, phi: Formula) -> Formula:
    """The modality `next` applied d times."""
    for _ in range(d):
        phi = nxt(phi)
    return phi


def depth(phi: Formula) -> int:
    """Modal depth: the number of nested one-step observations."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return 0
    if kind == "neg":
        return depth(phi[1])
    if kind == "conj":
        return max(depth(phi[1]), depth(phi[2]))
    if kind == "next":
        return depth(phi[1]) + 1
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


def evaluate(m: PSystem, phi: Formula, s: int) -> float:
    """Truth probability of phi at the world s of m."""
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return m.val[phi[1]][s]
    if kind == "neg":
        return 1.0 - evaluate(m, phi[1], s)
    if kind == "conj":
        return min(evaluate(m, phi[1], s), evaluate(m, phi[2], s))
    if kind == "next":
        return sum(m.step[s][t] * evaluate(m, phi[1], t) for t in range(m.n))
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Approximate analogies and the analogy distance
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def preserves_atoms(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does the renaming f of worlds preserve every atomic truth probability?"""
    if set(m.val) != set(n.val):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.val[p][f[s]] - m.val[p][s]) < 1e-9
        for p in m.val
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_cost(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Worst-case one-step overlap defect produced by the renaming f."""
    return max(
        overlap_defect(m.step[s], [n.step[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(m.n)])
        for s in range(m.n)
    )


def analogy_distance(m: PSystem, n: PSystem) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[int, ...] | None]:
    """The analogy distance and an optimal renaming attaining it.

    d(M, N) = min { analogy_cost(M, N, f) : f an atom-preserving renaming },
    with the junk value 1 (and no witness) if no such renaming exists.
    Brute force over all n! renamings; feasible for n <= 8.
    """
    assert m.n == n.n, "systems must have the same number of worlds"
    best: float = 1.0
    witness: Tuple[int, ...] | None = None
    found = False
    for f in permutations(range(m.n)):
        if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
            continue
        c = analogy_cost(m, n, f)
        if not found or c < best:
            best, witness, found = c, f, True
    return (best, witness) if found else (1.0, None)


def is_isomorphism(m: PSystem, n: PSystem, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Does f preserve atoms and carry the kernel of m onto that of n exactly?"""
    if not preserves_atoms(m, n, f):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(n.step[f[s]][f[t]] - m.step[s][t]) < 1e-9
        for s in range(m.n)
        for t in range(m.n)
    )


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The extremal two-state family
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exact_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two absorbing worlds; the atom holds at world 1 and fails at world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name="exact")


def leaky_system(eps: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eps leaks out of world 1 into the absorbing world 0."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [eps, 1.0 - eps]],
                   val={"a": [0.0, 1.0]}, name=f"leaky({eps})")


def geometric_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - eps) ** d


def linear_modulus(eps: float, d: int) -> float:
    return d * eps


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The Hennessy-Milner extremal family on n = 2m worlds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def nominal_uniform(m: int) -> PSystem:
    """Uniform kernel on n = 2m worlds, with one nominal atom per world."""
    n = 2 * m
    step = [[1.0 / n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"uniform({n})")


def nominal_tilted(m: int, eta: float) -> PSystem:
    """As above, but mass eta is moved from each 'negative' world to a
    'positive' one.  Worlds 0..m-1 are positive, worlds m..2m-1 negative."""
    n = 2 * m
    row = [1.0 / n + (eta if j < m else -eta) for j in range(n)]
    step = [list(row) for _ in range(n)]
    val = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)}
    return PSystem(step, val, name=f"tilted({n},{eta})")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The resolution gap
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def identity_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds, each with a self-loop; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="two loops")


def swap_system() -> PSystem:
    """Two worlds forming a 2-cycle; the single atom is true everywhere."""
    return PSystem(step=[[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]], val={"a": [1.0, 1.0]}, name="2-cycle")


def all_formulas(atoms: Sequence[str], max_depth: int) -> List[Formula]:
    """All formulas over the given atoms up to the given modal depth
    (a finite generating family: atoms, negations, conjunctions, nexts)."""
    level: List[Formula] = [atom(p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[Formula] = list(level)
    for _ in range(max_depth):
        new: List[Formula] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(nxt(phi))
            new.append(neg(phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(conj(phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Valuation = Dict[str, List[float]]
Formula = tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core machinery
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def truth_vector(step: Matrix, val: Valuation, phi: Formula) -> List[float]:
    n = len(step)
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return list(val[phi[1]])
    if kind == "neg":
        return [1.0 - x for x in truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])]
    if kind == "conj":
        a = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        b = truth_vector(step, val, phi[2])
        return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)]
    if kind == "next":
        v = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        return [sum(step[s][t] * v[t] for t in range(n)) for s in range(n)]
    raise ValueError(kind)


def analogy_distance(m: Matrix, mv: Valuation, n: Matrix, nv: Valuation
                     ) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[int, ...] | None]:
    size = len(m)
    best, witness, found = 1.0, None, False
    for f in permutations(range(size)):
        if any(abs(nv[p][f[s]] - mv[p][s]) > 1e-9 for p in mv for s in range(size)):
            continue
        c = max(overlap_defect(m[s], [n[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(size)])
                for s in range(size))
        if not found or c < best:
            best, witness, found = c, f, True
    return (best, witness) if found else (1.0, None)


def formulas_up_to(atoms: Sequence[str], max_depth: int) -> List[Formula]:
    level: List[Formula] = [("atom", p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[Formula] = list(level)
    for _ in range(max_depth):
        new: List[Formula] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(("next", phi))
            new.append(("neg", phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(("conj", phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Graded (counting) modalities, two-valued
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

GForm = tuple  # ("atom", p) | ("neg", f) | ("conj", f, g) | ("grade", k, f)


def gsat(step: Matrix, val: Valuation, phi: GForm, s: int) -> bool:
    kind = phi[0]
    if kind == "atom":
        return val[phi[1]][s] > 0.0
    if kind == "neg":
        return not gsat(step, val, phi[1], s)
    if kind == "conj":
        return gsat(step, val, phi[1], s) and gsat(step, val, phi[2], s)
    if kind == "grade":
        k = phi[1]
        count = sum(1 for t in range(len(step))
                    if step[s][t] > 0.0 and gsat(step, val, phi[2], t))
        return count >= k
    raise ValueError(kind)


def graded_formulas(atoms: Sequence[str], rounds: int, grades: Sequence[int]
                    ) -> List[GForm]:
    level: List[GForm] = [("atom", p) for p in atoms]
    out: List[GForm] = list(level)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        new: List[GForm] = []
        for phi in level:
            new.append(("neg", phi))
            for k in grades:
                new.append(("grade", k, phi))
        for i, phi in enumerate(level):
            for psi in level[i:]:
                new.append(("conj", phi, psi))
        level = new
        out.extend(new)
    return out

def nominal_pair(m_half: int, eta: float) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Valuation]:
    n = 2 * m_half
    uniform: Matrix = [[1.0 / n] * n for _ in range(n)]
    row = [1.0 / n + (eta if j < m_half else -eta) for j in range(n)]
    tilted: Matrix = [list(row) for _ in range(n)]
    val: Valuation = {f"w{j}": [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for i in range(n)]
                      for j in range(n)}
    return uniform, tilted, val


def study_hennessy_milner() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("STUDY 2.  Recovery from depth-one observations is Lipschitz with")
    print("          constant exactly n/2")
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"{'n':>4}{'eta':>10}{'depth-1 gap':>14}{'n*eta/2':>10}"
          f"{'d(U,T)':>10}{'ratio':>9}")
    for m_half in (1, 2, 3):
        n = 2 * m_half
        eta = 1.0 / (2.0 * n)
        uniform, tilted, val = nominal_pair(m_half, eta)
        gaps: Set[float] = {
            round(abs(truth_vector(uniform, val, ("next", ("atom", f"w{j}")))[s]
                      - truth_vector(tilted, val, ("next", ("atom", f"w{j}")))[s]), 12)
            for j in range(n) for s in range(n)
        }
        dist, _ = analogy_distance(uniform, val, tilted, val)
        predicted = n * eta / 2.0
        print(f"{n:>4}{eta:>10.5f}{max(gaps):>14.5f}{predicted:>10.5f}"
              f"{dist:>10.5f}{dist / eta:>9.2f}")
        assert len(gaps) == 1 and abs(max(gaps) - eta) < 1e-12
        assert abs(dist - predicted) < 1e-9
    print("  => every depth-one observation is off by exactly eta, yet the least")
    print("     achievable analogy defect is exactly n*eta/2: the ratio column is")
    print("     the Lipschitz constant n/2, and it cannot be lowered.\n")

def study_nominal_transport() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)

    print("=" * 72)

    print(f"  n = {n},  eta = {eta:.5f},  d(U,T) = {dist:.5f},  renaming = {f}\n")
    print(f"{'depth':>6}{'observed gap':>16}{'1-(1-d)^depth':>18}{'depth*d':>12}")
    phi: Formula = ("atom", "w0")

        phi = ("next", phi)
    print("  => the certified geometric bound holds at every depth and is never")
    print("     exceeded, while the linear relaxation is strictly weaker.\n")

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Valuation = Dict[str, List[float]]


def overlap_defect(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 - sum(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(p, q))


def atomic_type(val: Valuation, s: int) -> Tuple[float, ...]:
    """The vector of atomic truth probabilities at the world s, in a fixed
    atom order: two worlds are interchangeable by an atom-preserving renaming
    only if they have the same atomic type."""
    return tuple(val[p][s] for p in sorted(val))


def type_classes(val: Valuation, n: int) -> Dict[Tuple[float, ...], List[int]]:
    classes: Dict[Tuple[float, ...], List[int]] = {}
    for s in range(n):
        classes.setdefault(atomic_type(val, s), []).append(s)
    return classes


def renaming_cost(m: Matrix, n_sys: Matrix, f: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """Worst-case one-step overlap defect produced by the renaming f."""
    size = len(m)
    return max(
        overlap_defect(m[s], [n_sys[f[s]][f[t]] for t in range(size)])
        for s in range(size)
    )


def analogy_distance(
    m_step: Matrix, m_val: Valuation,
    n_step: Matrix, n_val: Valuation,
) -> Tuple[float, Optional[Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """Return (d(M,N), optimal renaming).

    Step 1  Partition both world sets into atomic types.  If the two type
            profiles differ, no atom-preserving renaming exists: return the
            junk value 1 with no witness.
    Step 2  Enumerate only the type-respecting bijections, i.e. independent
            permutations within each class.
    Step 3  Score each candidate by its worst-case row overlap defect and keep
            the minimum together with its argmin.

    Complexity: O( prod_i (n_i!) * n^2 ) where n_i are the type sizes.  In the
    nominal case every type is a singleton, so exactly one candidate survives
    and the cost is Theta(n^2).  Without informative atoms the bound degrades
    to O(n! n^2); this is unavoidable in general, since the case d = 0 with
    0/1 kernels contains graph isomorphism.
    """
    size = len(m_step)
    if len(n_step) != size:
        raise ValueError("systems must have the same number of worlds")

    m_classes = type_classes(m_val, size)
    n_classes = type_classes(n_val, size)
    if set(m_classes) != set(n_classes):
        return 1.0, None
    if any(len(m_classes[k]) != len(n_classes[k]) for k in m_classes):
        return 1.0, None

    keys = sorted(m_classes)
    blocks = [list(permutations(n_classes[k])) for k in keys]

    best: float = float("inf")
    witness: Optional[Tuple[int, ...]] = None
    for choice in product(*blocks):
        f: List[int] = [0] * size
        for k, images in zip(keys, choice):
            for s, t in zip(m_classes[k], images):
                f[s] = t
        c = renaming_cost(m_step, n_step, f)
        if c < best:
            best, witness = c, tuple(f)
    return best, witness

Formula = tuple  # ("atom", p) | ("neg", f) | ("conj", f, g) | ("next", f)


def depth(phi: Formula) -> int:

    if kind == "conj":

    if kind == "atom":

    if kind == "neg":

    if kind == "conj":
        a = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        b = truth_vector(step, val, phi[2])
        return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)]
    if kind == "next":
        v = truth_vector(step, val, phi[1])
        return [sum(step[s][t] * v[t] for t in range(n)) for s in range(n)]

                for s in range(size))
        if not found or c < best:

    return best, witness

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int]


def spanning_forest(nodes: Iterable[int], edges: List[Edge]
                    ) -> Tuple[List[Edge], List[Edge]]:
    """Split the edges into a spanning forest and the remaining chords,
    by union-find.  Cost O(|E| alpha(|V|))."""
    parent: Dict[int, int] = {v: v for v in nodes}

    def find(v: int) -> int:
        while parent[v] != v:
            parent[v] = parent[parent[v]]
            v = parent[v]
        return v

    tree: List[Edge] = []
    chords: List[Edge] = []
    for (u, v) in edges:
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            chords.append((u, v))
        else:
            parent[ru] = rv
            tree.append((u, v))
    return tree, chords


def tree_path(tree: List[Edge], src: int, dst: int) -> List[Edge]:
    """The unique path between two nodes in a forest, by breadth-first search."""
    adj: Dict[int, List[Tuple[int, Edge]]] = {}
    for e in tree:
        adj.setdefault(e[0], []).append((e[1], e))
        adj.setdefault(e[1], []).append((e[0], e))
    prev: Dict[int, Tuple[int, Edge]] = {}
    seen = {src}
    frontier = [src]
    while frontier:
        nxt: List[int] = []
        for v in frontier:
            for (w, e) in adj.get(v, []):
                if w not in seen:
                    seen.add(w)
                    prev[w] = (v, e)
                    nxt.append(w)
        frontier = nxt
    if dst not in seen and dst != src:
        raise ValueError("nodes are not connected")
    path: List[Edge] = []
    cur = dst
    while cur != src:
        p, e = prev[cur]
        path.append(e)
        cur = p
    return path


def cycle_basis(nodes: Iterable[int], edges: List[Edge]) -> List[List[Edge]]:
    """A cycle basis: one fundamental cycle per chord.  Its size is
    |E| - |V| + (number of components)."""
    node_list = list(nodes)
    tree, chords = spanning_forest(node_list, edges)
    return [[c] + tree_path(tree, c[0], c[1]) for c in chords]


def holonomy_audit(
    nodes: Iterable[int],
    defects: Dict[Edge, float],

    tolerance: float,

    """For each basis cycle report the accumulated defect and the holonomy

    edges = list(defects)

            "cycle": cyc,
            "total_defect": total,
            "holonomy_bound": bound,
            "exact": total == 0.0,
            "flagged": bound > tolerance,
        })
    return report

### A guided tour of the analogy distance on probabilistic transition systems

---

Two machines. The first is a weather model for a coastal town: from *sunny* it usually
stays sunny, occasionally slips to *rainy*; from *rainy* it usually stays rainy. The
second is a chemical reactor: from *stable* it usually stays stable, occasionally tips
into *runaway*; from *runaway* it usually stays runaway.

You do not need a meteorology degree to see that these are the same machine wearing
different clothes. Rename *sunny* to *stable*, *rainy* to *runaway*, and the probability
tables line up — nearly. The weather flips with probability $0.05$; the reactor tips with
probability $0.07$.

This page is about the two questions that gap raises.

> **How much can you trust a nearly-correct analogy?**
> **Is "nearly a renaming of" a genuine distance — and is there always a best renaming?**

Both have complete answers. Error compounds **geometrically**, not linearly, and the
distance exists, is always **attained**, and is a genuine metric whose zero set is exactly
isomorphism.

---

## 1. The setting: systems that flip coins

Fix a finite set of **worlds**. A *probabilistic transition system* consists of a
**kernel** — for each pair of worlds a number $M(s,t)\ge 0$, the probability of moving
from $s$ to $t$, with $\sum_t M(s,t)=1$ — and a **valuation** assigning to each atomic
proposition $p$ and world $s$ a truth probability $V(p,s)\in[0,1]$.

An observer speaks a *modal* language:
$$\varphi ::= p \mid \neg\varphi \mid \varphi\wedge\psi \mid \bigcirc\varphi,$$
with truth probabilities
$$\llbracket p\rrbracket(s) = V(p,s),\quad
\llbracket \neg\varphi\rrbracket(s) = 1-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(s),\quad
\llbracket \varphi\wedge\psi\rrbracket(s) = \min\bigl(\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(s),\llbracket\psi\rrbracket(s)\bigr),$$
$$\llbracket \bigcirc\varphi\rrbracket(s) = \sum_t M(s,t)\,\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(t),$$
the expected truth of $\varphi$ one step from now. The **depth** of a formula is the
number of nested $\bigcirc$'s — how far into the future the observer looks. Depth is the
currency of everything below.

<details>
<summary><b>Why truth probabilities always stay in $[0,1]$</b></summary>

By induction on the formula. Atoms are in $[0,1]$ by definition; $x\mapsto 1-x$ and
$\min$ both preserve $[0,1]$; and for the modality, nonnegativity is clear while
$$\sum_t M(s,t)\,\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket(t) \;\le\; \sum_t M(s,t)\cdot 1 \;=\; 1$$
because the kernel row is a probability vector. This innocuous fact turns out to be the
reason error *saturates* rather than growing without bound — see §3.
</details>

---

## 2. Measuring the mismatch: the overlap defect

Two probability distributions $P$ and $Q$ share the mass $\sum_t \min(P_t,Q_t)$. What is
left over,
$$\mathrm{od}(P,Q) \;=\; 1-\sum_t \min(P_t,Q_t),$$
is the **overlap defect**: the mass on which they disagree. A one-line computation shows
it equals $\tfrac12\sum_t|P_t-Q_t|$, the classical
[total variation distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_variation_distance_of_probability_measures).

An **$\varepsilon$-approximate structural analogy** from $M$ to $N$ is a bijection $f$ of
worlds that gets the atoms *exactly* right, $V_N(p,f(s))=V_M(p,s)$, and the dynamics right
to within $\varepsilon$:
$$\mathrm{od}\bigl(M(s,\cdot),\,N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr)\;\le\;\varepsilon
\qquad\text{for every world } s .$$
In words: *rename the worlds so that every row of the transition table lands within total
variation $\varepsilon$ of its counterpart.* An analogy of defect $0$ is an isomorphism.

{{algorithm:0}}

Before any theorems, get your hands dirty. Two systems live on the worlds $0$ (atom false)
and $1$ (atom true). Drag the sliders and watch three things at once: the row-wise overlap
defects, the resulting analogy distance, and — the punchline — how the truth probability of
"will the atom hold after $d$ steps?" drifts apart as $d$ grows.

Start with **Extremal leaking family** and follow the green curve. It sits exactly on the
blue one. That is not luck; it is sharpness, and §5 explains why.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

- *Extremal leaking family*: the green curve hugs the blue bound. Raise $\varepsilon$ and

## 4. The transport theorem

Here is the first main result.

> **Transport Theorem.** If $f$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximate structural analogy from
> $M$ to $N$, with $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, then for every formula $\varphi$ of depth $d$
> and every world $s$,
> $$\bigl|\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_M(s)-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_N(f(s))\bigr|
> \;\le\;1-(1-\varepsilon)^d .$$

The heart of it is a single recursion. Suppose the truth probabilities of $\varphi$ are
known to differ by at most $\delta$ everywhere. Compare the two one-step expectations, and
split the mass into the part the kernels *share* and the part they do not. On the shared
mass — at least $1-\varepsilon$ of it — the two expectations differ by at most $\delta$.
On the disagreeing mass — at most $\varepsilon$ — you can say nothing better than the
trivial bound $1$, because both observables live in $[0,1]$. Averaging,
$$\delta \;\longmapsto\; \delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta).$$
Start at $\delta_0=0$, iterate $d$ times, get $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$.

Read that map again. Each extra step of lookahead does **not** add a fresh $\varepsilon$
to the error you already have. It adds $\varepsilon$ of the error you *do not yet* have.
Ignorance compounds like interest on the remaining principal, and saturates at total
ignorance rather than sailing past it.

<details>
<summary><b>The full induction, case by case</b></summary>

*Atoms.* Both sides are equal by the atomic condition, and $1-(1-\varepsilon)^0=0$.

*Negation.* The difference merely changes sign; depth is unchanged.

*Conjunction.* Use the elementary inequality
$$|\min(a,b)-\min(a',b')|\le\max\bigl(|a-a'|,|b-b'|\bigr),$$
together with the monotonicity of $d\mapsto 1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, to lift both inductive
bounds to $\max(\operatorname{depth}\varphi,\operatorname{depth}\psi)$.

*Modality.* The one-step estimate: let $P$ be a probability vector, $Q$ nonnegative with
$\mathrm{od}(P,Q)\le\varepsilon$, and $g\le1$, $g'\ge0$ with $g-g'\le\delta\le1$
pointwise. Writing $m_t=\min(P_t,Q_t)$ and $M_0=\sum_t m_t\ge1-\varepsilon$,
$$\sum_t P_tg(t)-\sum_t Q_tg'(t)
=\underbrace{\sum_t m_t(g(t)-g'(t))}_{\le M_0\delta}
+\underbrace{\sum_t(P_t-m_t)g(t)}_{\le 1-M_0}
-\underbrace{\sum_t(Q_t-m_t)g'(t)}_{\ge 0}
\;\le\;\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta).$$
Apply this in both directions — legitimate because $\mathrm{od}$ is symmetric — and note
$\delta+\varepsilon(1-\delta)=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d+1}$ when
$\delta=1-(1-\varepsilon)^{d}$.
</details>

{{algorithm:2}}

## 5. Geometric, not linear — and exactly geometric

The natural guess is that $d$ nested observations cost $d\varepsilon$. That guess is
**true as a bound**, by Bernoulli's inequality $(1-\varepsilon)^d\ge1-d\varepsilon$. But it
is **never an equality** for $d\ge2$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$:
$$1-(1-\varepsilon)^d \;<\; d\varepsilon .$$
And yet the guess was not foolish — the two moduli agree to first order:
$$d\varepsilon-\bigl(1-(1-\varepsilon)^d\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\,\varepsilon^2 .$$

{{visualization:0}}

Is the geometric bound itself best possible? One two-state example settles it. Let the
**exact system** have two absorbing worlds $\mathsf T$ (atom true) and $\mathsf F$ (atom
false); let the **leaky system** be identical except that from $\mathsf T$ a mass
$\varepsilon$ leaks irreversibly into $\mathsf F$. Ask $\bigcirc^d a$. The exact system
answers $1$; the leaky one answers $(1-\varepsilon)^d$, since the process must survive $d$
independent chances to leak. The discrepancy is exactly $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$: the bound,
on the nose, at every depth.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 6. From "an analogy exists" to "the best analogy"

Now the ruler. For two systems on the same world set define
$$d(M,N)=\inf\{\varepsilon : \text{there is an } \varepsilon\text{-approximate analogy } M\to N\}.$$

An infimum invites the usual worry: is it achieved? Here it always is, and the reason is
disarmingly simple. The atomic condition is rigid — a renaming either preserves every
atomic value or it does not — and a finite world set has only finitely many renamings. The
infimum therefore ranges over a **finite** set of candidates, each with the cost
$$\mathrm{cost}(f)=\max_s\,\mathrm{od}\bigl(M(s,\cdot),N(f(s),f(\cdot))\bigr).$$

> **Attainment.** The infimum is a minimum: there is an atom-preserving renaming $f^\star$
> with $\mathrm{cost}(f^\star)=d(M,N)$, and it is an honest $d(M,N)$-approximate analogy.
> Hence an $\varepsilon$-approximate analogy exists **precisely when** $d(M,N)\le\varepsilon$.

{{algorithm:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the metric axioms come for free</b></summary>

Approximate analogies form a **groupoid graded by total variation**:

- the identity renaming is a $0$-analogy $M\to M$;
- if $f$ is an $\varepsilon$-analogy $M\to N$ then $f^{-1}$ is an $\varepsilon$-analogy
  $N\to M$ (the overlap defect is symmetric);
- if $f$ is an $\varepsilon_1$-analogy $M\to N$ and $g$ an $\varepsilon_2$-analogy
  $N\to K$, then $g\circ f$ is an $(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)$-analogy $M\to K$ (the
  triangle inequality for total variation).

Applying these three operations to *optimal* analogies gives $d(M,M)=0$,
$d(M,N)=d(N,M)$ and $d(M,K)\le d(M,N)+d(N,K)$ immediately. The axioms are not proved by
hand; they are read off from the algebra of analogies.

And the last axiom — separation — holds in the strongest sense:

> **The zero set is isomorphism.** $d(M,N)=0$ if and only if some atom-preserving
> renaming carries the kernel of $M$ exactly onto that of $N$.

One direction is clear. For the other, if $d(M,N)=0$ then the optimal renaming has zero
overlap defect at every world, and two probability vectors at total variation distance $0$
are equal — so the optimal renaming *is* an isomorphism. Therefore $d$ is a genuine
$[0,1]$-valued metric on isomorphism classes.
</details>

{{visualization:1}}

Combining the two halves gives the sharpest possible continuity statement. With the
optimal renaming,
$$\bigl|\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_M(s)-\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_N(f^\star(s))\bigr|
\;\le\;1-\bigl(1-d(M,N)\bigr)^{\operatorname{depth}\varphi},$$
and the constant cannot be improved, because on the leaking family
$$d(\text{exact},\text{leaky}(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon$$
exactly — the atomic valuation pins the renaming to the identity, and the worst-case
one-step defect is the leak itself. Since that same family attains the modulus, this *is*
the modulus of continuity, not merely an upper envelope for one.

---

## 7. Networks, cycles, and the holonomy of meaning

Real analogical reasoning traverses networks. One maps an epidemic onto a rumour, the
rumour onto a forest fire, the fire back onto the epidemic. Each hop is approximate.

Composition adds defects, so along a chain with local defects
$\varepsilon_0,\dots,\varepsilon_{k-1}$ the composite is an analogy of defect
$\sum_i\varepsilon_i$, and depth-$d$ transport costs
$1-\bigl(1-\sum_i\varepsilon_i\bigr)^d$. For a **cycle** the composite is a permutation of
the original worlds, and the drift it induces on truth probabilities is the **semantic
holonomy** of the loop: how far your meanings have wandered by the time the argument comes
home.

> **Exact cycles have trivial holonomy.** If every analogy in a closed loop is exact, then
> every modal observation returns to its original value. Consequently any interpretation
> that depends only on a world's modal theory is globally well-defined around the loop.

{{visualization:2}}

{{algorithm:3}}

The bound is not vacuous: a two-arrow loop of total defect $1$ can send a depth-one
observation from probability $1$ all the way to $0$.

---

## 8. How much observation does it take?

Transport says structure controls observation. Does observation recover structure?

**In general, no.** Take two worlds and an atom true at both. In the first system each
world has a self-loop; in the second the worlds swap. Every modal formula, at every depth,
has the same truth probability in both — the atom is certainly true everywhere, so
everything downstream is forced. Yet no renaming of two worlds turns two self-loops into a
$2$-cycle: the analogy distance is $1$, its maximum.

<details>
<summary><b>Counting does not rescue it — and what does</b></summary>

One might add **graded modalities**, "at least $k$ successors satisfy $\varphi$". On
*deterministic* systems with constant atoms this changes nothing: each world has exactly
one successor, so every counting question collapses to the same answer regardless of where
the arrows point, and every graded formula is uniformly true or uniformly false in both
systems. The self-loop/swap pair is deterministic, so grading leaves it untouched.

What *does* separate the pair is a self-referential observation — "is the current world a
possible successor of itself?", i.e. $M(s,s)>0$ — a
[fixed-point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_%CE%BC-calculus) property, invariant
under exact analogies but invisible to counting. The missing resolution is a fixed-point
phenomenon, not a multiplicity phenomenon.
</details>

**With names, yes — at depth one, with a sharp constant.** Call a system **nominal** if it
has one atom per world, true exactly there. Then the renaming is forced: an analogy must
send each world to the world with the same name.

> **Approximate Hennessy–Milner Theorem.** If two nominal systems on $n$ worlds have all
> depth-one truth probabilities within $\eta$, then the naming map is an
> $(n\eta/2)$-approximate structural analogy, so all depth-$d$ truth probabilities agree to
> within $1-(1-n\eta/2)^d$.

The factor $n/2$ is the price of converting an entrywise bound on observations into a
total-variation bound on kernels, and it is exactly right: for every even $n=2m$ there are
two nominal systems — one uniform, one with mass $\eta$ shifted from each "negative" world
to a "positive" one — whose depth-one observations differ by exactly $\eta$ at every pair,
and between which no analogy of defect below $n\eta/2$ exists. Recovery is Lipschitz with
constant exactly $n/2$.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 9. What it all adds up to

**Approximation error in iterated reasoning saturates.** Chaining $d$ inferences through a
model that is $\varepsilon$ wrong costs $1-(1-\varepsilon)^d$, not $d\varepsilon$. The
distinction is invisible for small $d\varepsilon$ and decisive for large: the linear
estimate happily predicts errors above $1$, while the truth approaches total ignorance and
stops.

**"Almost the same system" is a metric notion, and the optimum is realised.** The analogy
distance is a minimum over finitely many renamings, inherits the metric axioms from the
groupoid of analogies, and vanishes exactly on isomorphic pairs.

**Observation and structure are different resolutions of sameness.** Which notion of "the
same" you get depends on which questions you are allowed to ask. The analogy metric
measures structural sameness; modal truth measures behavioural sameness; and the gap
between them is exactly the content of the self-loop-versus-swap example.

Analogy, on this account, is not a vague literary gesture. It is an arrow in a groupoid,
weighted by total variation, transporting truth with a geometric loss, obstructed around
loops by a holonomy, and organising the space of systems into a bounded metric space whose
zero set is isomorphism. That is a lot of structure for an idea usually filed under
intuition.
